questions.stem: Which two structural properties must a problem have for DP to apply?
choices: Polynomial input size and bounded depth
questions.explanation: Optimal substructure lets you express OPT in terms of smaller OPTs; overlapping subproblems is what memoisation exploits.

questions.stem: If a problem has optimal substructure but NO overlapping subproblems, the natural technique is:
questions.explanation: Without overlapping subproblems there is nothing to memoise; divide-and-conquer recursion already runs in polynomial time.

questions.stem: What is the Weighted Interval Scheduling recurrence?
questions.explanation: Either include j (gain w_j, then jump to p(j)) or exclude j (recurse on j-1). Take the max.

questions.stem: What is p(j) in Weighted Interval Scheduling?
choices: The previous job in the input
The largest index i < j with f_i <= s_j
The job with smallest start time
The number of jobs that overlap j
questions.explanation: p(j) is the latest job that finishes before j starts — found via binary search after sorting by finish time.

questions.stem: The 0/1 Knapsack DP runs in time:
questions.explanation: Two indices (item count n, residual capacity w) give an n*W table; each cell does O(1) work.

questions.stem: Why is the O(nW) 0/1 Knapsack DP called pseudo-polynomial?
choices: It is polynomial in W's value but exponential in W's bit length (log W)
It runs only on small inputs
questions.explanation: Input size measures bits. O(nW) is exponential in log W, so polynomial in value but not in input length. Decision Knapsack is NP-complete.

questions.stem: What is the subproblem definition in Kadane's max-subarray DP?
choices: Max subarray sum of any subarray in A[1..i]
Max subarray sum ending exactly at index i
questions.explanation: OPT[i] must end at i, which yields the simple recurrence OPT[i] = max(OPT[i-1] + A[i], A[i]).

questions.stem: Which problem has the recurrence L[i] = 1 + max{L[j] : j < i, X[j] < X[i]}?
questions.explanation: L[i] is the LIS length ending at index i; we extend the longest LIS ending at a smaller value seen earlier.

questions.stem: After computing the DP table, how do you reconstruct which jobs are in the optimal Weighted Interval Scheduling solution?
choices: Walk back through the table comparing OPT(j) to OPT(j-1); include j when including improves
questions.explanation: At each j, decide which branch of the max was used: if w_j + OPT(p(j)) >= OPT(j-1), include j and jump to p(j); else jump to j-1.

questions.stem: Memoisation differs from tabulation in:
choices: Direction of computation (top-down recursive vs bottom-up iterative)
questions.explanation: Both achieve identical asymptotic time. Top-down memoisation skips unnecessary subproblems; bottom-up tabulation has tighter constants.

questions.stem: What is the naive (no memoisation) recursion time for Weighted Interval Scheduling?
questions.explanation: Two recursive branches per call yield Fibonacci-like growth Theta(phi^n) ~ 1.618^n. Memoisation reduces to polynomial.

questions.stem: In the 0/1 Knapsack recurrence, when w_i > w (current capacity), OPT(i, w) equals:
questions.explanation: If item i doesn't fit, the optimum is the same as the optimum without item i.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a step in the standard DP recipe?
choices: State the recurrence and base cases
questions.explanation: Sorting may appear in specific problems (Weighted Interval Scheduling) but is not a generic DP recipe step.

questions.stem: An optimal substructure means:
choices: The optimal solution decomposes into optimal solutions of subproblems
questions.explanation: Optimal substructure is the property that lets you write OPT in terms of OPT on smaller subproblems.

questions.stem: What is the space complexity of a straightforward 0/1 Knapsack DP?
questions.explanation: The 2D table is n*W entries; space can be reduced to O(W) by keeping only the last row, but the naive bound is O(nW).

questions.stem: Why is Weighted Interval Scheduling's DP O(n log n) total, despite linear DP work?
choices: Sorting by finish time and computing p(j) via binary search cost O(n log n); the DP itself is O(n)
Inputs are sorted in O(log n)
questions.explanation: Pre-sort + binary search for p(j) costs O(n log n); the DP sweep is linear. Total O(n log n).

questions.stem: When you write a DP, what is the FIRST artefact you produce?
questions.explanation: Every DP starts from a precise subproblem definition. Without it the recurrence is meaningless.

questions.stem: Which is a correct subproblem for Longest Increasing Subsequence in the O(n^2) DP?
choices: Length of longest increasing subsequence of X[1..i]
Length of longest increasing subsequence ending at index i
Length of any subsequence of X[1..i]
questions.explanation: Pinning the subsequence to end at i makes the recurrence local: L[i] = 1 + max over earlier compatible indices.

questions.stem: For 0/1 Knapsack, decision form (does a subset of value >= V fit?) is:
questions.explanation: Decision Knapsack is one of Karp's 21 NP-complete problems. The pseudo-polynomial DP doesn't contradict this.

questions.stem: Which DP would you use for 'is there a subset of {a_1, ..., a_n} summing to T'?
questions.explanation: Subset Sum has the same shape as Knapsack: subproblem indexed by (i, t). Pseudo-polynomial in T.

questions.stem: What does 'order of evaluation' mean in a bottom-up DP?
choices: The order that respects the dependency relation in the recurrence
questions.explanation: Subproblem c must be computed before any larger subproblem that depends on c. Typically smaller indices first.

questions.stem: When is a memoised top-down DP strictly faster than a bottom-up tabulated DP?
choices: Never — they have the same asymptotic complexity
When the dependency graph is sparse so many cells are not needed
When recursion is faster than iteration
questions.explanation: Both are the same asymptotically. Top-down can skip cells the answer doesn't depend on; bottom-up always fills the entire table.

questions.stem: If the recurrence OPT(j) requires both OPT(j-1) and OPT(p(j)), what is the cell evaluation order?
questions.explanation: Since OPT(j-1) and OPT(p(j) with p(j) <= j-1) are smaller indices, computing j = 1, 2, ..., n in increasing order respects dependencies.

questions.stem: Which technique is NOT typically used to reduce space in a DP?
choices: Keeping only the last one or two rows
Using bitmasks for the inner dimension
Replacing the table with a polylog factor of itself
questions.explanation: Greedy is not a space-reduction tactic; the other three are standard DP space optimisations.

questions.stem: Which BEST captures the difference between an algorithm with running time O(n + W) and O(nW)?
choices: O(n + W) is genuinely polynomial in input size only if W is at most polynomial in n; O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial in W
questions.explanation: Both depend on the value of W, but a fully polynomial-in-input algorithm must be polynomial in log W. O(nW) and O(n + W) are both pseudo-polynomial.
